pages.text: Fifth Canadian soldier dies from injuries caused by large fire at military base Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Fifth Canadian soldier dies from injuries caused by large fire at military base 3 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Ella Kipling Canadian Department of National Defence Pte William Douglas Dal Bianco died from his injuries suffered at a Canadian military base last month A fifth Canadian soldier has died from injuries he suffered when a grass fire swept through a military training area last month. Four people were killed initially and dozens were injured when the fire, which ignited during a live fire training exercise, spread rapidly through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright carried by strong winds on 17 October. Pte William Douglas Dal Bianco, who had been receiving medical care in Ontario, died on Friday, the Canadian Armed Forces said in a statement. Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote on X: "Canadians are holding Private Dal Bianco's loved ones, and all those still grieving in the wake of this terrible tragedy, in our hearts." The Canadian Armed Forces said that 24 military personnel were still in hospital receiving treatment, while 14 had been released as of Saturday. Thirty-eight military personnel had been injured in total. pages.text: Fighting for American Jobs Through Trade | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Fighting for American Jobs Through Trade The U.S. Department of Labor’s Bureau of International Labor Affairs (ILAB) fights to place American workers and businesses first in U.S. trade deals. We require countries that want access to U.S. markets and foreign investment to comply with international labor standards. This ensures U.S. workers and businesses don’t have to compete against bad actors who profit from cheap, exploited labor. ILAB oversees labor provisions in U.S. trade deals, preference programs, and other multilateral investments. We work with our trade partners to make sure they follow the rules, and we use every tool at our disposal to protect American jobs and enterprises from unfair competition abroad. Here’s how we do it: We fight for American workers and American jobs by demanding fair treatment in trade deals and rejecting trade partner labor practices that suppress wages and abuse workers. We negotiate high labor standards into trade deals, so U.S. workers aren’t undercut by foreign labor abuses that cost them wages or jobs. We direct trade partner investments in the United States toward American workers, including workforce development. We track our trade partners closely to make sure they’re living up to their labor commitments. We hold trade partners accountable when they break the rules—either by working with them directly or through strong enforcement actions. pages.description: Relentlessly hunted for its scales, the mysterious armored pangolin is vanishing throughout Africa. Now scientists are trying to unlock the secrets that could help save it.
pages.text: Fighting to Save the Pangolin, the World’s Most Wanted Animal | National Geographic By Henry Wismayer Photographs by Marcus Westberg Published September 23, 2026 It was 4 p.m. in the forests of central Cameroon, which meant it was time to wake the pangolins . The first resident roused from slumber occupied a wooden crate positioned against the wall inside an airy clinic. The animal that emerged was as unusual as it was enchanting: around three feet long, with a low-slung body, a narrow tapering head, powerful forelimbs tipped with curved claws, a prodigious tail. A pregnant white-bellied pangolin, one of the eight recognized species, she was accustomed to this routine by now, having arrived at the Tikki Hywood Foundation ’s pangolin rescue center a week earlier. She’d been rescued from a market in the nearby town of Mbalmayo; her bruised tail suggested that she’d been caught in a snare. Too vulnerable to go outside to forage for the ants and termites that constitute her natural diet, she was being sustained with maize meal mixed with supplements, and a sprinkling of soil, which helped trigger her instinct to feed and aided her digestion. The center’s Zimbabwean founder, Lisa Hywood, held out the bowl of porridge as the animal went to work with her noodle-like tongue. Filing a Significant New Use Notice (SNUN) under TSCA Overview Under section 5(a) of TSCA and 40 CFR part 721, if EPA promulgates a Significant New Use Rule (SNUR), a manufacturer or processor wishing to engage in a designated significant new use must submit a Significant New Use Notice (or "SNUN") to EPA at least 90 days before engaging in the new use. This notification provides EPA the opportunity to evaluate the new use and, if necessary, take action to prohibit or limit the activity. EPA recommends that submitters consult with the Agency prior to submitting a SNUN to discuss what data may be useful in evaluating a significant new use. Discussions with the Agency prior to submission can afford ample time to conduct any tests that might be helpful in evaluating risks posed by the substance. Filling the Strategic Petroleum Reserve Filling the Strategic Petroleum Reserve Established in 1975 in the aftermath of the OPEC oil embargo, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve was originally intended to hold at least 750 million barrels of crude oil as an insurance policy against future supply cutoffs (the maximum size was later reduced when a geologically unstable storage site was decommissioned). Today's design capacity is 714 million barrels. Direct Purchases Early fill of the SPR was primarily accomplished by purchasing crude oil on the open market. Concern over the vulnerability of the United States to additional oil cutoffs prompted the federal government to purchase most of the oil for the SPR in the late 1970s and early 1980s when world oil prices often exceeded $30 per barrel. Since that time, world oil prices have fluctuated from the mid-teens to record-breaking highs exceeding $100 per barrel during 2008. The average price per barrel for crude oil in the SPR reflects the value of the crude oil at the time it was acquired. Final Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM) On February 7, 2024, EPA strengthened the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM NAAQS) to protect millions of Americans from harmful and costly health impacts, such as heart attacks and premature death. ​Particle or soot pollution is one of the most dangerous forms of air pollution, and an extensive body of science links it to a range of serious and sometimes deadly illnesses. ​ EPA is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM 2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter to provide increased public health protection, consistent with the available health science. EPA is not changing the current: primary and secondary (welfare-based) 24-hour PM 2.5 standards, secondary annual PM 2.5 standard, and primary and secondary PM 10 standards. EPA is also revising the Air Quality Index to improve public communications about the risks from PM 2.5 exposures and making changes to the monitoring network to enhance protection of air quality in communities overburdened by air pollution. pages.text: Find Balance in Costa Rica’s Natural Treasures Skip to main content Sponsored Content by Costa Rica Find Balance in Costa Rica’s Natural Treasures Get inspired by Costa Rica’s abundant treasures and learn how this forward-thinking nation gave rise to the ecotourism movement Sponsored Content by From the crystal blue waters of the Caribbean Sea to the dense, lush forests of the mountains, Costa Rica has long been a destination for travelers who want to immerse themselves in the beauty of the natural world. Get inspired by Costa Rica’s abundant treasures and learn how this forward-thinking nation gave rise to the ecotourism movement. In August of 2020, Costa Rica will celebrate fifty years of its National System of Conservation Areas program, which over the last half-century has designated nearly 25 percent of the country as protected wildlife zones, and for good reason—five percent of the Earth’s biodiversity is found here. Almost thirty years ago the Costa Rican government launched an initiative to compensate landowners for protecting their forests, and it paid off—in the first 20 years of the program, the country's rainforest coverage increased by nearly 30%. And with 29 national parks, 19 wildlife refuges, and 8 biological reserves, there’s ample space to see the flora and fauna that make Costa Rica so special. Rainforests, volcanoes, and expansive beaches are all part of the Costa Rican landscape, and each location offers eco-friendly options that take sustainable travel to a whole new level. By Nicholas St. Fleur Published February 23, 2026 In fantasy books and movies, the undead rise from fire and ice. In the real world, mummies can emerge naturally from melting glaciers and dry desert caves. Others were created when bodies were slowly dried in smoke and ash. In this episode of Dead World , our new series about the most fascinating discoveries in archaeology and paleontology, we examine how extreme heat and cold preserved humans and animals for thousands of years. From Ötzi the Iceman locked in an Alpine glacier to smoke-dried human mummies in ancient Asia, desiccated desert cheetahs , and a frozen Siberian wolf cub carrying woolly rhino DNA in its gut, these discoveries reveal lost cultures and extinct animal populations. Through archaeological and genomic research, scientists are reconstructing their ancient lives. Watch the video and let us know what super-dead things we should cover next. Your new employer should provide you with a notice of your health coverage options and retirement plan. Consider enrolling in your employer's benefit plans. If your employer offers more than one health plan option – an HMO plan, a preferred provider option, and a fee-for-service plan, for example – compare each to your needs and preferences before making a decision. Ask for copies of two key documents – the Summary Plan Description (SPD) and the Summary of Benefits and Coverage (SBC) – to get details about covered benefits and costs. Find out what type of plan you have, how it works, and what eligibility requirements you may have to meet. Know what portion of your premium and costs you will pay, how much they will be, and who to talk to if you have questions. Another option to consider is enrolling in coverage through the Health Insurance Marketplace (Marketplace). The Marketplace offers health insurance plans that provide comprehensive health coverage that present their price and benefit information in an SBC so you can make comparisons. Keep in mind that with most job-based health insurance plans, your employer pays part of your premiums. If you pick a Marketplace plan instead, the employer usually doesn’t contribute to your premiums. pages.text: First on the scene: How community volunteers are helping crash victims on Bangladesh’s highways Skip to main content WHO Bangladesh Traffic on the Dhaka–Chattogram highway in Bangladesh, where trained community volunteers are helping provide first aid and emergency assistance to people injured in road traffic crashes. © Credits First on the scene: How community volunteers are helping crash victims on Bangladesh’s highways 4 November 2026 Reading time: Khokon is not a doctor or a paramedic. He is a shopkeeper who lives alongside the busy Dhaka–Chattogram highway in southeastern Bangladesh, where road traffic crashes regularly leave people dead or seriously injured. When a crash happens nearby, he may be among the first to arrive. Sometimes the call comes when he is at home. He finds a rickshaw or a car and rushes to the scene. He treats wounds, reassures frightened victims and contacts their families. If an injury is serious, he helps get the person to hospital. Long after the crash, some of the people he has helped come back to see him. “They tell me and the other volunteers, ‘Your help is unforgettable. We will remember this until our death,’” he says. “I feel happy and proud, I cannot express how much.” Khokon shares that pride with 119 other community first responders trained to improve emergency care for road crash victims through an initiative led by Bangladesh’s Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), with technical support from the World Health Organization (WHO). Build your confidence with things you know you can do, and then add new challenges. For example, a new physical activity could start with just 1 day per week, for as little as 5 to 10 minutes. As you go, you can add more minutes to your routine or challenge yourself to be active more days of the week. If you have more than one new habit in mind, start with one and add more habits after you’ve gotten a few weeks of practice. pages.text: Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda 1 day ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Olivia Ireland and Bethany Bell , Vienna Reuters Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals. Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements. The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin. Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said. The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024 . Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest". pages.text: Flaco Jimenez: Tiny Desk Concert : NPR Accessibility links Skip to main content Keyboard shortcuts for audio player Flaco Jimenez: Tiny Desk Concert Jimenez is part of a musical continuum that reaches from 19th-century Mexico all the way to The Rolling Stones. And he does it by playing waltzes on a button accordion. Flaco Jimenez: Tiny Desk Concert November 12, 2012 2:00 PM ET Felix Contreras Flaco Jimenez: Tiny Desk Concert Listen · 10:30 10:30 Toggle more options Download Embed Embed < iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/164958884/164790852" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player"> Credit: NPR Watching Flaco Jimenez play his button accordion is like looking back in time. His grandfather started playing an accordion in cantinas and family parties along the Texas/Mexican border around the late 1800s. Then Flaco's dad, Santiago Jimenez Sr., carried on the family tradition when he released his first record in 1936. Two of the songs you hear Flaco Jimenez play in this Tiny Desk Concert are traditional German polkas; they were popular in the mid-1800s as German immigrants settled in Texas before it became part of the U.S. almost 20 years later. Over time, the two-step stayed the same, but the German lyrics were replaced by the Mexican storytelling song form known as corridos. Sponsor Message But Jimenez is no dusty relic; he's very much of the here and now. FEMP provides guidance and assistance to help agencies implement federal legislative and regulatory requirements mandating reduced petroleum consumption and increased alternative fuel use. This includes planning for acquisitions of alternative-fueled vehicles, as well as installation of supply equipment to supply the energy these new vehicles require. This expansive network of waterways, including the designated Wild & Scenic Noatak River, stretches over 400 miles from the Brooks Range to the Chukchi Sea. Renowned for their pristine waters and remote locations, these rivers invite visitors to immerse themselves in the beauty of the region. The most floated rivers in Noatak National Preserve include the Noatak River, the Kelly River , and the Kugururok River . In this capacity, she leads a team of about 90 Federal and contractor staff responsible for administrating and overseeing a management and operating contract with an annual budget of approximately $3 billion, a workforce of more than 8,000 people, and several billion dollars in government-owned facilities and assets. Ms. Tindle is responsible for implementing national security and nonproliferation missions by providing oversight of program management, nuclear operations, security, quality assurance, environment, safety, and health, and the execution of key mission deliverables at NNSA’s Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. She is a member of the Senior Executive Service. Before joining NNSA, Ms. Tindle was Vice President of Engineering Excellence at Lockheed Martin. pages.description: Most dengue infections cause mild flu-like symptoms or no symptoms at all. But at least one person has died from this year’s outbreak in Florida, where health experts worry the disease will become more common in the future
pages.text: Florida Is Facing Its Worst Dengue Outbreak in Decades, With at Least 524 Locally Acquired Cases. Here's What to Know Skip to main content Dengue is a viral disease transmitted by mosquitoes. Joao Paulo Burini via Getty Images This year, the Florida Department of Health has recorded a staggering 524 locally acquired cases of dengue , a mosquito-borne viral disease, as of October 31. That’s the highest number recorded there since the disease returned to the state in 2009 , according to Forbes ’ John Drake. For context, only 62 locally acquired cases were documented in 2025. Most infected people either do not show symptoms or experience only mild illness . But in early September, a Tampa-area woman named Gay Rabb Small died of dengue on her 80th birthday, after developing a tremor and going to the emergency room, per the New York Times ’ Anemona Hartocollis. Later that month, three counties in Florida declared local emergencies over the illness, and in October, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a national emergency response to dengue. “It is very unusual to have transmission in the United States,” Eva Harris , an infectious diseases expert at the University of California, Berkeley, tells the Times . “This is so very much of an eye-opener.” Here’s what to know about dengue. What is dengue? Dengue is a viral disease spread by mosquitoes, mainly the species Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus , which are both present in Florida , among other places.
